primitives.name: Signed Measure Finiteness
primitives.verbatim_quote: If E and F are measurable sets and μ is a signed measure such that then |μ(E)| < ∞.
primitives.assumptions: μ is a signed measure on a ring, E ⊆ F, μ(F) is finite.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When μ(F) = ±∞, leading to undefined or infinite μ(E).

layer2.mapping: GSI uses this kernel to validate finite expectation bounds in probabilistic models.
layer2.telemetry: Verification of finite signed measure on measurable subsets.

primitives.name: Additive Structure of Signed Measures
primitives.verbatim_quote: It follows from the definition of signed measures, just as for measures, that a signed measure is finitely additive and, therefore, subtractive.
primitives.assumptions: μ is defined on a ring of sets, E, F are disjoint or nested.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Failure of finite additivity leads to non-subtractive behavior.

layer2.mapping: GSE maps additive structure to state transition logic in discrete dynamical systems.
layer2.telemetry: State transition consistency under signed measure decomposition.

primitives.name: Absolute Convergence of Series
primitives.verbatim_quote: If μ is a signed measure and {En} is a disjoint sequence of measurable sets such that |μ(Un-1 En) |< ∞, then the series ∑n-1 μ(En) is absolutely convergent.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Infinite sum of μ(E_n) without absolute convergence.

layer2.mapping: GSI leverages absolute convergence for stable predictive inference.
layer2.telemetry: Convergence rate of signed measure series in probabilistic forecasting.

The core insight of signed measures lies in their ability to extend the notion of measures to include infinite values while preserving key structural properties such as finite additivity and subtractivity. This allows for a unified treatment of positive and negative contributions in integration theory. The proof of finiteness relies on the additive property: μ(F) = μ(F − E) + μ(E), where if either term is infinite, so is μ(F). The only remaining case is when both terms are finite, ensuring that all measurable subsets of finite-signed-measure sets also have finite signed measure. Absolute convergence arises from the requirement that the total variation of a signed measure must be finite for the series to converge. These principles underpin both probabilistic modeling and state-space dynamics in GSI and GSE respectively.
